articles.title: Dam burst, lake overflow, earthquake: Nepal faces fresh crisis as rescue operations halted
articles.summary: China News: Kathmandu: Nepal’s rescue operations were temporarily halted for 90 minutes on Friday after a landslide-formed lake on the Nepal-China border began ov.
articles.body: Kathmandu: Nepal’s rescue operations were temporarily halted for 90 minutes on Friday after a landslide-formed lake on the Nepal-China border began overflowing, triggering fears of another surge in the flood-ravaged region. The fresh alert came as a magnitude 5.1 earthquake struck China’s Sichuan province, adding to the mounting challenges facing the disaster-hit Himalayan region.Lake overflow triggers fresh flood alertA lake formed by debris from the massive glacier collapse began overflowing on Friday, raising fears of renewed flooding in communities already devastated by Wednesday’s flash floods.Nepal warned rescue teams to move to safer locations after authorities received information that the glacial lake had breached its banks. The Nepal Army subsequently suspended rescue operations for one hour and 30 minutes as authorities assessed the threat.Residents in Rasuwa district, near the border with China's Tibet, were seen rushing towards higher ground as the river level began rising, according to a Reuters witness."We can see that the level of water in the river is rising," Narendra Pariyar, the senior-most bureaucrat in Rasuwa district, said, adding that authorities were still assessing the situation.The rising water also prompted Chinese rescue personnel and vehicles to withdraw to a designated safe area, state broadcaster CCTV reported.Barrier lake holds millions of cubic metresThe lake was formed when debris from the glacier collapse blocked the river, creating a natural barrier and trapping water upstream.China mobilised an eight-member engineering team on Thursday to conduct aerial surveys and three-dimensional modelling of the lake. By Friday, the reservoir had grown to more than 2.5 million cubic metres, compared with an estimated 1.5 million to 2 million cubic metres a day earlier.Authorities fear that a breach could send another powerful surge downstream, threatening communities that are already struggling to recover from the earlier disaster.The latest crisis comes after a huge torrent of rock, ice, mud and debris tore through Himalayan river systems following the collapse on Wednesday.Death toll climbs as rescue efforts disruptedThe confirmed death toll in Nepal has risen to 469, while almost 1,000 people remain missing in Nepal and Tibet. At least 540 foreigners are among those reported missing.The floods swept through villages and valleys, destroying power stations, roads and bridges along a key route connecting Kathmandu with Lhasa in Tibet. The corridor is also popular with trekkers and pilgrims travelling towards Mount Kailash.Before the latest suspension, Nepalese rescue teams had been using helicopters to search for survivors and deliver emergency supplies to thousands of people cut off in towns and valleys. Emergency workers, including teams using sniffer dogs, had also recovered dozens of bodies swept downstream into the plains.Dibga Tamang was among the last people rescued from Rasuwa on Thursday, when he was airlifted with three others to an army camp in Nuwakot."All of our people have gone. They are dead," Tamang said. "I have no one left waiting for me. Everything and everyone is gone. The end."Nepal says it does not need foreign rescue teamsDespite offers of assistance from several countries, Nepal has said it does not currently require foreign search-and-rescue teams."The offer for help is natural. Our security agencies are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don’t require such help,” Lok Bahadur Chhetri, spokesperson for the foreign ministry said on Friday.A South Korean rapid response team is already in Kathmandu but has not been deployed because Nepal has yet to establish a plan to accept foreign rescue teams, according to South Korea’s foreign ministry.China border crossing devastatedThe disaster has also caused extensive destruction around the Gyirong border crossing on the Chinese side. Chinese rescuers had yet to reach the worst-hit area as crews worked to clear debris from the access road.Dramatic footage from Wednesday showed torrents of muddy water and debris tearing through structures at the border crossing within seconds.CCTV reported that 558 people were missing in Tibet’s Gyirong County, including 260 foreign nationals. Three people have been confirmed dead on the Chinese side.Chinese Premier Li Qiang visited the disaster-hit area in Gyirong on Thursday as rescue and relief operations continued.Magnitude 5.1 earthquake hits ChinaAdding to the uncertainty in the region, a magnitude 5.1 earthquake struck Longchang City in Neijiang, Sichuan province, on Friday, according to the China Earthquake Networks Center.There were no immediate reports of casualties or damage from the earthquake.The fresh seismic event comes as authorities remain on alert across the Himalayan region, where rescue teams are already dealing with unstable terrain, blocked rivers and the risk of further landslides and flooding.Families wait for news of missingThe disaster has triggered a desperate search for missing relatives across several countries. Among those unaccounted for are dozens of Americans who had travelled from Nepal towards Tibet’s Mount Kailash.President Donald Trump said the United States had offered assistance to Nepal."Nobody's ever seen anything quite like that, where very powerful, strong, well-built buildings were wiped out like they were toothpicks. It's a terrible thing. We are sending aid and we've spoken to the leadership and we let them know anything they want, they'll have."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: By 2008, Michael Forbes had refused £450,000 for his 23-acre home: Trump’s £1bn Scottish golf resort was moving ahead around him
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Michael Forbes had already turned down Donald Trump’s offer of up to £450,000 for his 23-acre property at Mill of Menie when Scottish ministers approv.
articles.body: Michael Forbes had already turned down Donald Trump’s offer of up to £450,000 for his 23-acre property at Mill of Menie when Scottish ministers approved Trump’s proposed golf resort in November 2008. The small farm near Balmedie, north of Aberdeen, sat inside the much larger Menie Estate that Trump wanted to turn into a golf and residential development. Forbes and his wife, Sheila, refused to move, leaving their property surrounded by a project that Scottish ministers had now given permission to proceed. The episode had started as a property dispute, and by late 2008, it had become one of the most closely watched local conflicts surrounding the American developer’s Scottish plans. The Guardian reported on November 3, 2008, that the proposed £1bn coastal resort would cover about 2,000 acres and include two 18-hole championship courses, a hotel, timeshare apartments, homes, villas and other facilities. Forbes’ 23-acre holding remained inside the development area.Forbes was sitting on land Trump wantedTrump had acquired much of the Menie Estate in 2006 and soon announced plans for a major golf development along the Aberdeenshire coast. Forbes’ family had longstanding connections to the property, and he had lived there for decades. He worked as a fisherman and quarry worker and maintained the farm with his wife. Trump’s representatives approached Forbes about selling, and the offers increased over time. By 2007, the figure had reached £450,000, according to contemporary reporting, with the possibility of a job also discussed.Forbes still refused, and the dispute became more personal in October 2007 after Trump publicly attacked the condition of Forbes’ property. Trump described the land as a “disgrace” and “disgusting”, while Forbes made clear that he had no intention of leaving. At that stage, however, Trump’s wider development was not guaranteed. In November 2007, Aberdeenshire councillors rejected the resort proposal after a close vote, and the planned development had faced opposition from environmental groups and some local residents because parts of the site were considered environmentally sensitive. The Scottish Parliament later examined the planning process, and its official record shows that representatives of the Trump Organization appeared before the Local Government and Communities Committee in February 2008 as the dispute over the Menie development continued.The planning battle moved beyond the local councilThe Scottish Government became involved, and the project went through a public inquiry during 2008, and Forbes’ property remained one of the central complications. Trump wanted to build a large resort around land he did not control, while Forbes continued to reject the offers. The 2008 plans called for two championship golf courses, a 450-room hotel, hundreds of holiday apartments, 500 homes and 36 villas. The development also included a golf academy and facilities for workers.Supporters argued that the resort would bring investment and tourism to the region. Opponents raised concerns about the coastal dunes and the environmental effect of construction. The Scottish Government ultimately sided with the development. On November 3, 2008, Scottish ministers confirmed outline planning permission. The decision included conditions covering environmental protection, public access and other aspects of the project.The Guardian reported that Trump’s offers for the property had reached £450,000 and that Forbes and his wife were still refusing to move. Their farm buildings, tractors and home would remain amid the much larger development.Construction could continue without buying Forbes outTrump no longer needed to win another local planning vote before proceeding with the resort, although detailed planning work and environmental conditions still had to be addressed. The development was not designed around Forbes’ property; instead, the resort would rise around it. That created a weird arrangement: a large commercial golf project could proceed while a small private holding remained inside its boundaries. By December 2008, Trump’s team had begun working on the detailed design of the resort. The Guardian reported that plans included a 500-home housing estate, 36 luxury villas, a 450-bed hotel and high-rise timeshare accommodation. The newspaper also reported that construction might not begin until 2010.Trump’s organization also considered whether compulsory purchase powers could eventually be used against some remaining properties, although Forbes’ refusal did not prevent the golf course itself from going ahead. The first Trump International Golf Links course at Menie eventually opened in 2012, several years after the planning approval that had allowed the project to move forward.The resort expanded while Forbes remainedSome of the large residential elements proposed in 2008 did not materialize as originally described, while the golf operation became the central part of the Menie development. The Scottish Government's records show that the Menie Estate became a five-star golf resort, and the Trump Organization later developed a second course on the property. In July 2025, the Scottish Government said Donald Trump was in Aberdeenshire for the official opening of that second course at Trump International.That later development is separate from the 2008 planning battle, but it shows how the site changed after the original approval. Forbes’ refusal therefore did not stop the resort. Nor did Trump’s plans remove the small property that had become the most visible obstacle to his original vision. It initially began with offers for a 23-acre farm, and became a long-running dispute over land, development and the limits of a major private project. The golf resort eventually opened and expanded, while the property at the centre of the 2008 standoff remained part of the story of Menie.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Jakarta unrest: Protests turn violent, transport services disrupted after overnight clashes
articles.summary: South Asia News: Transport services in parts of Jakarta were disrupted on Friday following overnight unrest near Indonesia’s parliament, with local media reporting rio.
articles.body: Transport services in parts of Jakarta were disrupted on Friday following overnight unrest near Indonesia’s parliament, with local media reporting rioting in the area. Several commuter rail services were suspended or rerouted, while bus operations near parliament were affected by road closures. Some toll roads in the vicinity were also shut.The protests began near parliament on Thursday morning amid a heavy security presence. Various groups demonstrated against government policies and demanded tougher punishment for corrupt officials. Thousands of police personnel had been deployed across Jakarta ahead of the rallies.Overnight unrest follows parliament protestAfter the main rally ended on Thursday evening, local media reported that people wearing black shirts remained near the protest site. They allegedly blocked roads and threw rocks and sticks at police before setting fire to a police post and two motorcycles.Police responded with water cannon and tear gas as the unrest escalated.A Reuters witness reported hearing several loud bangs near the site. Jakarta police initially did not issue a statement and did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Jakarta police spokesperson Budi Hermanto later confirmed that rioting had taken place, according to local media.“Acts of vandalism can disrupt social order and stability,” detik.com quoted him as saying.65 arrested after unrestPolice said 65 people were arrested on Thursday on suspicion of attempting to create unrest. Authorities said they seized air guns and communication devices, as well as materials allegedly intended for making Molotov cocktails.Videos circulating on social media early Friday appeared to show police using tear gas, with officers crouching behind shields. Reuters said it could not immediately verify the footage.The protests were held on the anniversary of last year's deadly anti-government demonstrations, which continued for two weeks and posed an early challenge to President Prabowo Subianto's administration.Prabowo faces pressure over economyThe latest unrest comes as Prabowo seeks to rebuild confidence among the public, businesses and investors concerned about the economic impact of his ambitious populist programmes.Prabowo, a retired general, won the 2024 presidential election with a large majority. However, concerns have grown over the cost of his policies and their impact on the economy.A poll conducted by investigative news outlet Tempo put his approval rating at 38 per cent this month.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Indian-origin Miami developer Rishi Kapoor sentenced to over 11 years in $89 million fraud case
articles.summary: US News: Rishi Kapoor, a Miami real estate developer of Indian origin, has been sentenced to 11 years and 4 months after pleading guilty to a large-scale fraud scheme involving $89 million and numerous investors. Kapoor mismanaged funds and failed to remit payroll taxes, resulting in significant financial harm to investors and the IRS.
articles.body: A Miami real estate developer of Indian origin has been jailed for 11 years and four months in prison after pleading guilty to money-laundering and payroll-tax conspiracy charges linked to an $89 million fraud scheme involving investors in his South Florida property projects, according to Miami Herald.Rishi Kapoor, 42, was sentenced on Thursday by US District Judge K. Michael Moore in federal court in Miami. Kapoor, the former CEO of Location Ventures and URBIN, told the court that he had acknowledged his “sins and crimes” and apologized to investors, former employees and his family for the harm he had caused.“I fully accept responsibility for my crimes without hesitation or excuse,” Kapoor wrote in a letter to the judge before sentencing.Kapoor was arrested in March on a 37-count federal indictment. Prosecutors said he raised at least $89 million from more than 50 investors for South Florida residential projects and owed at least $70 million in restitution to those investors. At least another $800,000 was owed to the Internal Revenue Service.The case centred on Location Ventures projects in parts of South Florida including Coconut Grove, Miami Beach, Coral Gables and Fort Lauderdale. Prosecutors alleged that money raised for individual developments was diverted for other purposes, including Kapoor's personal expenses.Kapoor pleaded guilty in May to conspiring to defraud the United States by failing to remit payroll taxes withheld from employees' wages for Social Security and Medicare between 2020 and 2022. According to the indictment, he also failed to file personal federal income-tax returns from 2019 through 2023.He also pleaded guilty to a money-laundering charge involving $820,559 transferred from his personal bank account as a down payment towards the purchase of a $5 million, 68-foot Princess yacht in 2022.The two charges to which Kapoor pleaded guilty carried a maximum combined sentence of 15 years.Prosecutors recommended that Kapoor serve 136 months in prison. His lawyers had sought a 121-month sentence, or just over 10 years, which they said was at the lower end of the applicable sentencing guidelines.Kapoor's defence also disputed prosecutors' description of the case as an $89 million fraud scheme. His lawyer Don Samuel told the court that Kapoor himself had earned about $6 million over the relevant eight-year period, including his salary from Location Ventures.“This is not a Ponzi scheme,” Samuel said. “He was not swindling anybody.”Prosecutor Elizabeth Young argued that Kapoor had raised the $89 million through “fraudulent misrepresentations” and used funds intended for one real estate project to finance another.The original federal indictment accused Kapoor of using investor money intended for real estate developments for personal expenses and other purposes. Prosecutors previously alleged that several promised condominium projects were never completed, including developments in Coconut Grove and Miami Beach.Court documents also accused Kapoor of withholding payroll taxes from employees and failing to send the money to the IRS. Prosecutors alleged that around $2 million in payroll taxes was retained rather than remitted.Kapoor was also accused of making misleading statements to banks while seeking money for the yacht and other expenses. Prosecutors said he told investors he had contributed about $13 million of his own money to the ventures, while the actual amount was roughly half that figure.The indictment further alleged that Kapoor deceived escrow agents to obtain the release of pre-construction condominium deposits and then diverted the money to personal expenses unrelated to the developments.Kapoor had built a profile in South Florida's real estate and political circles through his companies and had ties to the mayors of Miami and Coral Gables. His criminal case followed a separate Securities and Exchange Commission civil enforcement action in 2024 involving another alleged fraud scheme. Kapoor agreed to pay restitution in that matter without admitting wrongdoing.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Nepal floods: Morgues overflow with bodies, authorities turn to dry ice, electric crematorium
articles.summary: South Asia News: Nepal is facing a grim challenge after the devastating Bhotekoshi floods, with bodies being recovered across several districts and morgues running out.
articles.body: Nepal is facing a grim challenge after the devastating Bhotekoshi floods, with bodies being recovered across several districts and morgues running out of space.Bodies recovered from Rasuwa and Nuwakot have been found as far downstream as Chitwan, Tanahun and Nawalparasi. Authorities are transferring remains to neighbouring districts as hospitals struggle to accommodate them.Air conditioners, temperature-controlled rooms and dry ice will be used to slow decomposition. If needed, the electric crematorium at Devghat will also be used, according to a report by the Kathmandu Post.In Chitwan, 137 bodies had been recovered from stretches of the Trishuli and Narayani rivers between Phishling and Golaghat by Thursday morning. A temporary storage centre is being prepared in Bharatpur with a capacity for around 250 bodies.The disaster has also left families searching for missing relatives, with people arriving from Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Gorkha carrying photographs in the hope of identifying recovered remains.Pokhara is also struggling. Ninety-three bodies have been brought there from Tanahun, Gorkha, Nawalparasi East and Dhading, while hospitals across Kaski can accommodate only 88 bodies.“By the numbers, we are already above capacity,” Kaski chief district officer Kuman Singh Gurung said as quoted by The Post He added that nearby districts may have to be used if more bodies arrive.Authorities are racing against decomposition. Bodies at Pokhara Academy of Health Science are being stored at 2-6°C, but officials say this can preserve them for only around 10 days to two weeks. Longer-term storage would require sub-zero facilities, which Pokhara currently lacks.Police are photographing bodies, collecting fingerprints and DNA samples and conducting post-mortems to help with identification. Unidentified remains may eventually be buried at designated sites, with tags and records maintained for possible identification later.The pressure is mounting in other districts too. Gorkha, Nawalparasi East and Dhading have transferred bodies to Pokhara, Kathmandu and other neighbouring areas after exhausting local storage capacity.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1931, scientists last documented this mysterious lark; 95 years later, birders photographed one alive in Chad
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A bird missing from scientific records for nearly a century has been rediscovered in central Chad, turning a long-standing mystery into one of Africa’.
articles.body: A bird missing from scientific records for nearly a century has been rediscovered in central Chad, turning a long-standing mystery into one of Africa’s most remarkable recent ornithological findings. The Rusty Lark (Calendulauda rufa) was documented on 2 February 2026 in the Abou Telfane wildlife reserve in Guéra province, where a Franco-Chadian team observed, photographed and filmed the elusive species. According to Tour du Valat’s account, the sighting is the first documented record since 1931 and produced the first known photographs of a living Rusty Lark. Birds of the World’s report also highlights the significance of finding a species that had remained extraordinarily poorly documented despite its presence across the Sahel.Rusty lark rediscovered in Chad after nearly a century without a confirmed recordThe historic observation took place on 2 February 2026, when Idriss Dapsia of Chad’s Directorate of Wildlife and Protected Areas, Julien Birard of Tour du Valat and Pierre Defos du Rau of the French Office for Biodiversity encountered the Rusty Lark in the Abou Telfane wildlife reserve, around 10 kilometres east of Mongo. Tour du Valat reports that the same individual was seen again on 15 February. The discovery ended a 94-year gap in confirmed records. The last documented record dated to 1931, meaning generations of ornithologists had no verified modern observation of the species. Crucially, the team captured photographs and video, providing physical evidence that could be independently examined. Experts including Joost Brouwer, Tim Wacher, Paul Donald and Per Alström subsequently confirmed the identification from the field images.Why the first photographs of the Rusty Lark are so importantThe rediscovery is particularly significant because the Rusty Lark had remained one of Africa’s least understood birds. Although it was never officially declared extinct, its extraordinary lack of records made its continued survival difficult to assess. The species is associated with dry Sahelian environments across countries including Niger, Chad and Sudan, regions where extensive areas remain poorly surveyed. The photographs taken in Chad therefore provide more than an exciting record. They offer researchers the first detailed visual evidence of a living Rusty Lark that can be compared and studied. According to Tour du Valat, expert ornithologists in Chad and specialists in larks examined the images and confirmed the identification. Birds of the World’s coverage further places the discovery within the broader effort to locate bird species that have disappeared from scientific observation. The finding demonstrates how targeted fieldwork can still reveal major biodiversity surprises in remote landscapes.What the Rusty Lark rediscovery reveals about Sahel biodiversityThe discovery also raises important questions about where the Rusty Lark lives, how many individuals survive and why it remained undetected for so long. Its apparent survival does not automatically mean the species is abundant. The Search for Lost Birds account notes that the bird is considered generally scarce, while much of its potential range receives limited ornithological attention. The Chad sighting could therefore encourage further surveys in suitable habitats and potentially help researchers reassess the species’ known distribution. The observation also demonstrates the value of international conservation partnerships. Tour du Valat says the discovery occurred through the RESSOURCE+ project, coordinated by the FAO and co-financed by the European Union and FFEM, bringing together Chadian and French specialists. For conservationists, the rediscovery is a reminder that species can remain hidden in under-surveyed ecosystems for decades, making continued field research essential to understanding Africa’s remaining biodiversity.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: US judge blocks Trump admin's Anthropic sanctions, calls them unlawful
articles.summary: US News: A US federal judge has ruled that the Trump administration acted unlawfully in targeting AI firm Anthropic after it resisted certain military uses of .
articles.body: A US federal judge has ruled that the Trump administration acted unlawfully in targeting AI firm Anthropic after it resisted certain military uses of its models, saying national security cannot be used to justify retaliation against government critics.US District Judge Rita Lin said the government’s decision to designate Anthropic as a “supply chain risk” was unlawful and violated the company’s constitutional rights, according to the BBC.“The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics,” Lin said in her 59-page ruling.The ruling blocks federal agencies named in Anthropic’s lawsuit from enforcing President Donald Trump’s directive restricting the use of the company’s Claude AI tools.It also overturns former Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth’s decision to classify Anthropic as a supply-chain risk — a designation generally used against companies linked to countries considered security threats.The decision makes permanent an earlier temporary suspension of the sanctions and takes effect immediately. The administration can challenge the ruling before a higher court.Anthropic welcomed rulingAnthropic welcomed the court decision, saying it remained committed to working with the US government on national security applications of AI.“We welcome the court’s ruling that this supply chain risk designation was unlawful,” an Anthropic spokesperson said, according to the BBC.The dispute began after Anthropic refused to allow its AI models to be used for fully autonomous lethal weapons and mass surveillance of Americans.The company argued that its models were not sufficiently reliable for safe deployment in weapons systems and that domestic surveillance could violate constitutional rights.Trump had sharply criticised Anthropic, describing it as a “radical left, woke company” and accusing it of trying to control military activity through its terms of service.Lin said the government's actions appeared to be aimed at punishing Anthropic for challenging the administration rather than addressing a genuine national security threat.In an earlier stage of the case, she had said the government appeared to be trying to “cripple” the company and “chill public debate” over military use of AI.The Pentagon had designated Anthropic as a supply-chain risk earlier this year, marking the first publicly known instance of an American company receiving such a designation.Anthropic faces separate Pentagon actionThe latest ruling does not resolve all of Anthropic’s legal disputes with the Pentagon. A separate action taken by the Defence Department under federal procurement rules remains in effect, with that matter still awaiting a final ruling.Anthropic’s AI systems had also been used by the US military in classified and sensitive operations, according to reports cited by the BBC.The legal victory comes as Anthropic prepares for a potential stock market debut, which could become one of the biggest technology listings if it goes ahead.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. It had to circle the London airport to get rid of excess fuel ahead of the unscheduled landing.The United Airlines flight eventually landed at Heathrow without issues about two and a half hours after departing Venice. articles.title: Nepal-China border: Why a newly-formed lake is sparking fears of more flooding
articles.summary: South Asia News: Rescue operations continued through thick layers of mud and debris in flood-hit Nepal on Friday, while authorities remained on high alert after a newl.
articles.body: Rescue operations continued through thick layers of mud and debris in flood-hit Nepal on Friday, while authorities remained on high alert after a newly formed lake near the Nepal-China border began overflowing, raising fears of another flash flood.The warning comes two days after devastating floods swept through the Himalayan border region, killing more than 500 people and leaving over 1,500 missing.Nepal's disaster management authorities said satellite imagery and preliminary assessments indicated that a river had been blocked upstream, creating a growing lake that could burst and send a sudden surge of water downstream.The rescue operations were also disrupted for some time after the newly formed barrier lake began overflowing, raising fears of another flash flood in areas already devastated.Where is the newly formed lake?Satellite imagery shown by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV indicated that the lake had formed in the same area where a glacial detachment occurred on Wednesday, triggering the chain of events that caused widespread destruction downstream.CCTV reported that the lake's barrier was more than 10 km from Gyirong Port, a key border crossing with Nepal that was inundated by mud and floodwater.The lake is located at an elevation of about 2,950 metres, nearly 1,000 metres above Gyirong Port.How did the lake form?The lake was formed after debris from a massive glacier collapse blocked the river near the Nepal-Tibet border, creating a natural barrier and trapping water upstream. Debris and rocks blocked part of the river, creating a temporary natural dam and causing water to accumulate behind it.The lake is located near the confluence of the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers. Both rivers originate in Tibet and merge before entering Nepal, where the combined river is known as the Bhote Koshi, which later flows into the Trishuli river.The lake had already begun overflowing, with Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) warning that it could continue to grow and potentially burst.“The lake is continuing to grow and there is a risk that it could burst,” the NDRRMA said."Another dammed lake was formed by the August 26th ice-rock avalanche and this has begun to outflow," Qianggong Zhang of the International Center for Integrated Mountain Development said, the Associated Press reported.Zhang said the lake contains a few million cubic metres of water and is located in a valley with a limited elevation drop towards downstream areas. The volume of water is equivalent to roughly 1,200 Olympic-sized swimming pools.Why are authorities worried?Scientists have warned that continued glacial melt, high temperatures and debris blocking river channels could lead to further flooding."There is still a lot of glacial melts going on because of high temperatures and the water is accumulating at various points, as there is bound to be a lot of debris and rock on the river’s path," said Jakob Steiner, a geoscientist at the University of Graz in Austria.Both Zhang and Steiner said the warnings should be taken seriously, particularly as rescue teams continue searching for people missing in the floods. However, they said another flash flood on the same devastating scale was unlikely.India monitoring situationWednesday's flash floods swept through villages and valleys, destroying roads, bridges and hydropower infrastructure along a key route linking Kathmandu with Lhasa in Tibet. The area is also frequented by trekkers and pilgrims travelling towards Mount Kailash.At least 320 Indians remain missing, while around 400 others are stranded on the Chinese side following the floods along the Nepal-Tibet border, the ministry of external affairs (MEA) said in a media briefing.MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India was ready to provide all possible assistance to Nepal in its rescue efforts. He said 96 Indian nationals stranded on the Chinese side had safely crossed into Nepal by land.Twenty-one Indians also arrived in New Delhi on Friday, a day after reaching Kathmandu from the flood-affected areas of Nepal, PTI reported.Since Wednesday night, India has also sent a total of 47.5 tonnes of emergency supplies to Nepal in two military transport aircraft and is in the process of sending more relief materials.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Two resignations, same scam: Why B Nagendra quit Karnataka cabinet again
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Karnataka minister B Nagendra announced his decision to resign from the state cabinet on Friday, just 25 days after assuming office, amid m.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Karnataka minister B Nagendra announced his decision to resign from the state cabinet on Friday, just 25 days after assuming office, amid mounting pressure over his alleged involvement in the Maharshi Valmiki Scheduled Tribe Development Corporation financial irregularities. Addressing a press conference, teary-eyed Nagendra said that he was innocent and had been unfairly targeted by the opposition."I am resigning of my own will to avoid the embarrassment that may cost my party because of unnecessary allegations made by the opposition party against me," Nagendra said."Manuwadis (apparently referring to the BJP) targeted me as they didn't want a tribal person in the country to grow," he added.This comes after Bharatiya Janata Party and JD(S) had been demanding Nagendra's resignation over the alleged scam and had planned a foot march from Raichur to Ballari from September 1 to 10.The opposition had also staged repeated protests inside and outside the Karnataka Vidhan Saudha during the monsoon session, which was curtailed by three days and adjourned sine die on August 24 amid the continued uproar.Second resignation in over two yearsThis is Nagendra's second resignation from the cabinet over the same allegations. Earlier, in June 2024, Nagendra had resigned from the tribal welfare department in Siddaramaiah's cabinet after the controversy had surfaced.He was, however, re-inducted into DK Shivakumar's cabinet on August 3, 2026, with the planning and statistics portfolio, prompting the opposition to revive its demand for his removal.What is Valmiki scam?The Valmiki scam refers to the alleged illegal transfer of funds from the Karnataka Maharshi Valmiki Scheduled Tribes Development Corporation Ltd, a state-run body under the administrative control of the minister’s department.The alleged irregularities came to light following the suicide of accounts superintendent Chandrashekhar P on May 26, 2025. In his death note, Chandrashekhar alleged that Rs 187 crore belonging to the corporation had been unauthorisedly transferred from its bank account.Of this amount, Rs 88.62 crore was allegedly moved to various accounts, including those linked to prominent IT companies and a Hyderabad-based cooperative bank.The matter gained further momentum after Union Bank of India filed a complaint with the CBI, which subsequently registered an FIR and began investigating the alleged financial irregularities.Following the development, then chief minister Siddaramaiah and then state Congress president DKS reportedly met and sought the resignation of Nagendra, promising reinstatement if he was found not guilty.The state government also constituted a Special Investigation Team (SIT), headed by Manish Kharbikar, additional director general of police, economic offences, at the Criminal Investigation Department (CID), to conduct a parallel probe.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A Houston lawyer bought a 15,000-sq-ft mansion listed for $15.5 million just to demolish it; he plans to donate about $4 million of its materials and turn the land into a garden
articles.summary: US News: Prominent Houston trial lawyer Tony Buzbee has bought a 15,000-square-foot luxury mansion listed for $15.5 million in the exclusive River Oaks neighbo.
articles.body: Prominent Houston trial lawyer Tony Buzbee has bought a 15,000-square-foot luxury mansion listed for $15.5 million in the exclusive River Oaks neighbourhood, with plans to tear down the entire house and turn the property into a private garden estate. The purchase of 1708 River Oaks Boulevard allows Buzbee and his wife, Frances Moody Buzbee, to expand their existing property directly beside their long-time home at 1722 River Oaks Boulevard. Instead of living in or renovating the large mansion, the couple has partnered with Habitat for Humanity to remove and save usable materials from the property before demolition begins.Reports from the Houston Business Journal and the Houston Chronicle confirmed that the non-profit will manage the salvage work, recovering millions of pounds of architectural fittings and building materials to support affordable housing projects across Texas. “They will be tearing it down and salvaging approximately $4 million worth of high-end materials, appliances, air units and the like for their mission,” Buzbee said in an email statement about the donation. “They are excited to have it, and we are proud to support them.”Salvaging luxury fixtures for charityUnder the agreement with Habitat for Humanity, salvage crews will carefully remove materials from inside and outside the 15,000-square-foot mansion before the site is cleared. The recovery work will include high-end kitchen equipment, custom woodwork, marble fittings, large air-conditioning units and other building materials. The donated materials are estimated to be worth $4 million. Habitat for Humanity plans to use some of the recovered items in affordable housing projects, while specialised fixtures may be sold through its ReStore shops to raise money for its work. Once the house is removed, the property will become a large private garden. The new green space will connect directly with the family’s main home next door, effectively doubling the size of their landscaped grounds along one of Houston’s best-known streets.Property value and River Oaks historyThe purchase reflects continued activity in River Oaks, an 1,100-acre master-planned community founded in 1924 by brothers Will and Mike Hogg and Hugh Potter. The neighbourhood remains one of Houston’s most exclusive residential areas and is controlled by strict deed restrictions and private maintenance rules overseen by the River Oaks Property Owners association. Harris Central Appraisal District records reviewed by Zillow show that 1708 River Oaks Boulevard had an assessed value of $18,062,181 in 2026. Official tax records show that the property had an annual tax bill of $383,861 before the sale. The $15.5 million asking price was therefore considerably below the official assessed value. Real estate publication The Real Deal said the purchase fits a growing trend known as landmaxxing. The term describes wealthy homeowners buying neighbouring properties, removing existing buildings and combining the lots into larger private estates.A history of high-profile property movesBuzbee, a former United States Marine Corps officer who ran for Houston mayor in 2019, has had a prominent presence on River Oaks Boulevard since buying his first home at 1722 River Oaks Boulevard for $14 million in 2013. In 2017, Buzbee drew widespread attention after buying a fully operational, demilitarised $600,000 World War II Sherman tank that had taken part in the Normandy landings. He parked the tank along the kerb outside his home, leading to a dispute with the local property owners association. He eventually donated the tank to Texas A&M University in 2018. The main estate also became the scene of a major police investigation in 2019 after burglars broke into the home following a Super Bowl event. They stole $21 million worth of artwork, jewellery, firearms and electronics. The items were later recovered after Buzbee offered a $50,000 reward for information that led to arrests. In February 2022, the couple put their 12,209-square-foot Tudor-style mansion on the market for $27.5 million through Douglas Elliman Real Estate. PaperCity Magazine and CultureMap Houston reported at the time that the listing even allowed buyers to pay in Bitcoin. When the home failed to sell at that price, the family decided to keep it and expand onto the neighbouring property instead.Creating a larger private gardenThe demolition of 1708 River Oaks Boulevard will remove a mansion that included six bedrooms, an indoor swimming pool, a domed stained-glass ceiling, a lacquered library, a wine vault and a wellness wing with a beauty salon. Removing a fully functioning estate of this size is one of the more notable residential site clearances in recent Texas real estate. The work will happen in stages, starting with Habitat for Humanity’s salvage operation. Once workers have removed all usable fixtures and mechanical equipment, heavy machinery will bring down the remaining structure. Landscaping crews will then begin work on the garden extension. The finished project will join the two River Oaks lots into one large, connected green property. The expansion will give the family greater privacy while also sending millions of dollars worth of reusable construction materials towards charitable housing projects.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump discovers two more things he can rename - Lakes, and his place in history
articles.summary: US News: The TOI correspondent from Washington: In what was widely seen as part trolling and part wishful fantasy, MAGA supremo Donald Trump on Friday declared.
articles.body: The TOI correspondent from Washington: In what was widely seen as part trolling and part wishful fantasy, MAGA supremo Donald Trump on Friday declared himself in a social media post to be the “greatest” president in US history, ahead of George Washington, Abraham Lincoln, Franklin Roosevelt and others (who in his view were merely great).The bizarre and provocative post, viewed by some of his own supporters as excessively narcissistic, came hours after Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America” amid an increasingly testy relationship with Canada. In another post, Trump listed five presidents, including himself, Washington, Lincoln, Jefferson, and Reagan, as the ones who built America. The five who broke it? Buchanan, Wilson, Carter, Obama, and Biden -- all Democrats.Even MAGA principals are starting to wince at the 80-year old President’s increasingly surreal social media posts. Critics – some of whom believe his unvetted aide Natalie Harp is responsible for the torrent of rubbish – are wondering meanwhile if he can, or should, last out his term, often invoking the 25th amendment that allows replacing an incapacitated president.Several commentators called his post “delusional” and “pathetic” and attention-seeking, pointing out that in reality a poll of historians and scholars ranked Trump dead last and the worse president in history. “Usually you allow other people to say how great you are. But as soon as you start saying, I'm the greatest, that usually means that you suck,” one political analyst sneered on a tv show.Earlier, Trump turned one of North America’s Great Lakes into the latest casualty of his increasingly aggressive war against nouns. Following up his earlier transformation of the Gulf of Mexico into the Gulf of America, he changed Lake Ontario’s name to Lake America, a makeover that delighted his MAGA flock that embraces such frivolities as “trolling” and “owning the libs.” He also offered a tantalizing clue to what could be next: the Atlantic and/or Pacific oceans (stand-by Indian Ocean).Trump’s fascination with renaming things is part of a larger obsession with names and ratings, brands and branding. To the real-estate developer turned president, apparently nothing is quite complete until it has his or his chosen nameplate on it. Buildings need his name, as do golf courses, universities, airports, steaks, and wines.The Kennedy Center has provided the most engaging example of this branding impulse, with Trump-aligned trustees repeatedly seeking to put his name on the Washington performing-arts institution despite a federal judge ruling that the board overstepped its authority. Trump loyalists say the Center risks being demolished if his name is not attached to the refurbished building.The nomenclatural scrap over Lake Ontario though provides a delicious historical irony: the name predates both the United States and Canada, deriving, according to Canadian PM Mark Carney, from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.”Which essentially leaves the descendants of European colonizers and conquerors – the British, French and assorted later immigrants who eventually created the U.S and Canada – engaged in a spirited argument over what to call a lake whose original name came from people who were here before any of them. Rather like two tenants fighting over the correct name for a house while the original owner is sidelined.Indeed, America is littered with Indigenous names. Mississippi comes from an indigenous word associated with the great river. Across the US, states including Michigan, Minnesota, Kansas, Oklahoma, Nebraska, Wisconsin, Wyoming, Ohio, Massachusetts and Connecticut bear names rooted in the languages of Native Americans (who were themselves misidentified as “Indians.”). So do names such as Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, and Quebec in Canada, not to mention dozens of towns and rivers and settlements across the continent. And Trump, apparently, wants to solve this historical complexity with a Sharpie – while blowing his own Trumpet.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: IDF kills Hamas-linked former senior Jenin terror cell member in West Bank vehicle strike
articles.summary: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu congratulated the IDF for the "successful thwarting of the terrorists in Jenin" in an X/Twitter Post earlier on Friday. The...
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu congratulated the IDF for the "successful thwarting of the terrorists in Jenin" in an X/Twitter Post earlier on Friday.

The IDF killed a former senior Jenin terror cell member and two additional terrorists in an IAF airstrike on their vehicle in the West Bank on Friday, the military confirmed in a joint statement with the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency).

The senior terrorist, Qais Bitwani, was a Hamas operative in the now-dismantled Jenin terrorist network, according to the joint statement.

Qais Bitwani was a relative of the former Jenin terrorist network commander, Noor Bitawi, who was killed by the IDF in May 2025, the military and security agency said.

The statement noted that Qais Bitwani was involved in "significant" terror activities, including "directing, funding, and executing" terrorist attacks against Israeli soldiers and civilians.

Bitwani had maintained his connections to Hamas in the Gaza Strip, as well as international operatives, the statement added.

According to the IDF and Shin Bet , the other two terrorists in Bitwani's vehicle were his accomplices, and the vehicle also contained weapons.

Strike followed extensive intelligence effort

The Jerusalem Post has learned that the strike against Bitwani, who was formerly Hamas's top operative in the Jenin terrorist network, was conducted following an extensive intelligence effort led by the Shin Bet and the Military Intelligence Directorate.

The effort included arresting and interrogating dozens of Bitwani's accomplices who were suspected of being in contact with him, leading to his eventual discovery and targeting.

The Post further learned that Bitwani was directly involved in the July 2024 Gilboa Seam bombing, in which two Defense Ministry employees were injured, as well as additional attacks against Israeli soldiers and civilians. Several prior efforts were made to arrest Bitwani prior to the strike amid his continued terrorist activities.

Netanyahu, Israel Katz congratulate IDF for Jenin strike

Defense Minister Israel Katz also congratulated the IDF in an X post later on Friday, as well as the Israel Police and security forces, describing the strike as among the "fruits of the offensive and proactive policy we are leading in Judea and Samaria."

"We do not wait for terrorism," said Katz. "We pursue it, conquer its strongholds, and thwart its people."

He noted that the policy has led to an 80% decrease in West Bank terrorist activity, emphasizing that Israel "will continue to act forcefully and proactively to thwart any threat to its citizens, wherever it may be found."

Yonah Jeremy Bob contributed to this report.

articles.title: In 1993, Tim Curry bought a Los Angeles home for $650,000 as it faced demolition and spent years restoring it; hours after news of his death, the $7.5 million home found a buyer
articles.summary: Real Estate News: Tim Curry’s historic Los Feliz home has come under offer just hours after news of the actor’s death at 80 was announced. The property, which Curry pai.
articles.body: Tim Curry’s historic Los Feliz home has come under offer just hours after news of the actor’s death at 80 was announced. The property, which Curry painstakingly restored during his ownership, had been listed for $7.5 million and has now been marked as “contingent,” according to Realtor.The status means the seller has accepted an offer, although certain conditions still need to be met before the sale can officially close.The Los Angeles property has a remarkable Hollywood history. Curry purchased the home for $650,000 in 1993 and spent several years restoring it, eventually showcasing the transformation in Architectural Digest.Tim Curry bought the Los Feliz home in 1993Originally built in 1922, the historic residence was designed by acclaimed architect Stiles O. Clements. Known today as the Seyler House, the property features Spanish-inspired architecture and distinctive period details.Curry was drawn to the house after moving to Los Angeles from the UK. His friend and fellow actor Annie Potts reportedly took him to see the property, and the actor quickly felt that it could become the home he had envisioned.Curry recalled that he made an offer almost immediately after seeing the house. However, he soon learned that another potential buyer had withdrawn from the deal after a psychic allegedly told her that the house was haunted.“I soon learned that the previous bidder had been told by her psychic that the house was haunted and had just withdrawn from escrow,” Curry recalled.The rumor did not deter him.How Tim Curry transformed the historic propertyCurry spent years carefully restoring the house while adding his own eclectic design touches. He drew inspiration from a trip to Ireland, where he visited an estate belonging to the Guinness family.Describing the experience, Curry recalled it as the most beautiful and comfortable house he had ever visited. He was particularly inspired by its collection of paintings, aged surfaces and the layers of history created by generations of residents.He brought a similar philosophy to his Los Feliz home, preserving original elements such as exposed wood-beam ceilings, hand-painted surfaces, stained-glass windows, iridescent copper and vintage tiles.The property later appeared in Architectural Digest in 1998, documenting Curry’s meticulous restoration.A Hollywood home owned by several famous starsCurry eventually sold the Los Feliz property for $2.6 million in 2001. But his connection to Los Angeles real estate did not end there. He went on to renovate several other residences in the city, including one that he later sold to actress Christina Ricci.His former Los Feliz residence, meanwhile, passed through the hands of several prominent names.The property's later owners included former NBA star Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, The Pitt actor Noah Wyle, Twilight star Robert Pattinson, The Big Bang Theory actor Jim Parsons and Breaking Bad star Aaron Paul.According to the current listing, Paul worked with Commune Design in 2019 to update the property while preserving its historic character.Inside Tim Curry’s former Los Angeles homeThe approximately 4,000-square-foot home has four bedrooms and 3.5 bathrooms. Its interiors retain the warm, textured aesthetic associated with Curry's restoration, with several rooms featuring rich, dramatic colours.The home includes a dark persimmon dining room, a soft green living room and a dark teal den. The kitchen features bold green cabinetry, while the primary bedroom combines soft green walls with heavy patterned curtains and a tapestry.One of the property's most unusual features is a secret passageway leading to a speakeasy hidden behind a combination vault.The listing describes the interiors as a refined interpretation of Spanish Colonial design while highlighting the home's playful and unexpected details.The sprawling grounds include a pool, koi pond and gardensBeyond the main residence, the property sits on an expansive 1.45-acre lot filled with gardens and outdoor entertaining areas.The grounds include a freeform swimming pool, fire pits, a koi pond, cold plunge, spa and natural amphitheatre. There are also several intimate outdoor spaces and winding paths connecting different sections of the gardens.The property offers views toward the Downtown Los Angeles skyline, creating a contrast between its secluded, garden-like setting and its location in the middle of the city.Curry once described his approach to the home as being similar to designing a set for the life he wanted to live.“It’s rather like designing a set for the life you wish to pursue,” he said. “When I truly had a place that I wished to call home, I wanted it to be equally marvelous for my great friends, the other ‘cast members.’”Tim Curry dies at 80 after decades in HollywoodCurry, best known for playing Dr. Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Picture Show, died at his Los Angeles home at the age of 80. His longtime manager and friend Marcia Hurwitz confirmed his death, with no cause disclosed.The actor suffered a major stroke in 2012 and subsequently used a wheelchair, but continued working in the entertainment industry.Curry's career spanned stage, film and television. He earned three Tony nominations for Spamalot, My Favorite Year and Amadeus, along with an Emmy nomination.He became a cultural icon after portraying Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Picture Show, which began as a stage production in London in 1973 before moving to Broadway and then becoming the celebrated 1975 film.He also appeared in films including Home Alone 2: Lost in New York, where he played the memorable hotel concierge.Reflecting on his acting choices, Curry told the Associated Press in 1993, “I like playing the more curious corners of the human mind and human behaviour, partly because they’re a tad more interesting.”Now, as Curry's former Los Feliz residence moves toward a potential new chapter under a new owner, the historic home remains one of the most distinctive pieces of real estate connected to the late actor's extraordinary Hollywood legacy.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Quebec governing party: Trump is ‘real adversary’
articles.summary: Quebec governing party leader Christine Fréchette labeled President Trump as a “real adversary” as she launched her election campaign Thursday, citing the escalating trade war between the U.S. and Canada. “My opponent is named Donald Trump,” said Fréchette, who leads the right-leaning Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ). “He’s the real adversary.” Fréchette took over the CAQ…
articles.body:
Quebec governing party leader Christine Fréchette labeled President Trump as a “real adversary” as she launched her election campaign Thursday, citing the escalating trade war between the U.S. and Canada.

“My opponent is named Donald Trump,” said Fréchette, who leads the right-leaning Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ). “He’s the real adversary.”

Fréchette took over the CAQ in April after former Quebec Premier François Legault stepped down, putting her at the helm of a party that has governed the province for the past eight years. The October election will be her first test with voters as party leader.

On Thursday, Trump signed an executive order changing the name of Lake Ontario, which is shared between New York and Ontario, to “Lake America” in his latest move targeting Canada after failed trade negotiations .

Fréchette said she is seeking to guide Quebec through the economic uncertainty caused by the tit-for-tat tariffs between the nations, arguing her government would be best positioned to protect businesses and workers in the province.

“I’m asking for a mandate to move forward through a storm,” she said.

After Canada backed out of trade negotiations with the U.S., Trump imposed 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian imports.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, in turn, set retaliatory “dollar for dollar” tariffs on the U.S. effective Sept. 8. Trump later responded by imposing additional tariffs on Canadian automobiles starting Jan. 1.

Canadian independence has become a major focal point in the province’s election following Trump’s repeated threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state.

Fréchette’s main competitor in the race, Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, pushed back on Fréchette’s attempt to put Trump at the center of the race.

“Let’s not let the tariffs of Donald Trump’s administration confiscate this important debate from us,” he said. “Let’s not let him confiscate our election. “

articles.summary: India News: ZEHANPORA (BARAMULLA):  Excavations will begin Saturday on the second phase of Zehanpora, a Buddhist site in north Kashmir’s Baramulla. J&K chief .
articles.body: ZEHANPORA (BARAMULLA): Excavations will begin Saturday on the second phase of Zehanpora, a Buddhist site in north Kashmir’s Baramulla. J&K chief secretary Atal Dullo will inaugurate the project.The presence of a 2,000-year-old Buddhist civilisation at the site was discovered last year by Mohamad Ajmal Shah, a professor at University of Kashmir. It gained prominence after PM Narendra Modi mentioned it during his monthly radio programme Mann Ki Baat on Dec 28 last year.The Prime Minister recalled that people had noticed tall mounds in Zehanpora for years without knowing about their significance. What were first believed to be unusual rock formations were later found to resemble three Buddha stupas seen in photos in a French museum.According to Modi, the blurred photos, thousands of kilometres away, proved crucial as it showed three Buddhist stupas, helping archaeologists connect the dots and reconstruct Kashmir’s ancient past. The discovery reaffirms J&K’s rich cultural legacy.It all began in Oct 2023 when Shah was on a fellowship in France and came across the 100-odd old photos at Guimet Museum showing stupa domes in Baramulla. “I immediately realised I had visited the site. What struck me was the domes in the photos looked much larger than what we see now,” said Shah, attached to the varsity’s department of Central Asian Studies.Later, Shah requested J&K govt’s department of archaeology to fund the project and it agreed. Shah and his team started digging in Nov last year, initially discovering a hall identified as an apsidal (semi-circular) stupa.Shah and his team also found iron/copper artefacts, needles, decorated objects and other materials. “We identified wall alignments through drone images and excavated precisely at those points. There is a strong possibility that many structures and artefacts still lie preserved beneath the ground,” Shah said.Shah highlighted the possibility that the site was linked to the Fourth Buddhist Council (1st century CE). “Kashmir was a major centre of Buddhism in ancient times. It was here that Hinayana Buddhism evolved into Mahayana Buddhism, giving the religion a new philosophical and cultural form,” he said.Shah pointed out that the Chinese explorer Hiuen Tsang had mentioned Baramulla in his travel accounts. According to Shah, Tsang spent a night at Uskur, a Buddhist site near Baramulla town and visited several monasteries in the area. “This suggests Tsang must have visited the monastery at Zehanpora as well,” Shah said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Greenland says findings on forced contraception genocide allegation not final
articles.summary: Experts examined the use of forced contraception on the Inuit community during the 1960s and 70s.
articles.body:
Greenland's justice minister has said the government cannot conclude whether genocide was committed against the Inuit community after experts examined the use of forced contraception in the 1960s and 70s.

"We cannot say, on behalf of the government, whether there was genocide," Marianne Paviasen told reporters. "This is something we can continue to debate."

Two reports on the practice were released on Friday, a year after Denmark apologised for the treatment of Inuit women and girls in its autonomous territory.

Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said a "reconciliation commission" would be set up while Danish PM Mette Frederiksen promised the governments would work together.

Denmark has passed a compensation law to pay 300,000 Danish crowns (£34,404; $46,800) to each woman affected by the policy.

Records from the national archives show that, between 1966 and 1970, 4,500 Greenlandic women and girls, some as young as 13, had an intra-uterine device (IUD) implanted under a birth-control programme administered by Danish doctors.

In recent years, many women came forward to say they had been fitted with an IUD without their knowledge or consent.

Use of the birth control was so widespread that Greenland's population growth severely slowed.

Frederiksen issued an apology last August to Greenlandic women and their families affected by "systematic discrimination".

In 2024, a former prime minister of Greenland, Mute B Egede, described the practice as "genocide".

Under the UN Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide , one definition of genocide is "imposing measures intended to prevent births" within a "national, ethnical, racial or religious group".

The territory tasked a panel of four experts with establishing whether human rights had been violated and whether such violations met the definition of genocide.

However, the panel split, with two members resigning and producing a separate report.

The two experts who remained, Alaskan lawyer Dalee Sambo Dorough and University of Copenhagen law professor Miriam Cullen, found in their report that the rights of Inuit women in Greenland had been violated.

But they said that they could not conclude that genocide had taken place "on the basis of contraceptive practices alone".

They added that genocidal intent by Denmark remained a "possible inference" that a court might establish, based on evidence that fell outside the scope of their report, such as the removal of Inuit children to be raised by Danish families.

The rival report, produced by Jonas Christoffersen, former head of the Danish Institute for Human Rights, and Jensine Nedergaard, a psychologist who had worked in Greenland, accepted that women had been wronged but could not establish the extent of their mistreatment.

They found no evidence "any authority or health professional at any time had any intention of destroying the Greenlandic population".

Reacting on Friday, Greenland's justice minister said the two reports were so different that one "says there was no genocide at all" while the other "says there could have been".

Greenland contraception scandal victims hear Danish PM's emotional apology

Denmark apologises to Greenland's forced contraception victims

‘Doctors fitted a contraceptive coil without my consent’

One woman affected by the forced contraception policy, Henriette Berthelsen, told news agency AFP before the reports were presented that their conclusions had been skewed from the start because no Greenlandic Inuits had been appointed as experts.

"For me, this is not just about history or politics. It's my body, my life and my right to self-determination," she said.

"And once again, I see that it is others who will investigate and define what was done to me and to other Inuit women."

Another woman, Inger Platou, 70, told Reuters that she remembered waking up from what she had been told was a minor operation to discover an IUD had been inserted without her consent.

"It turns out we were treated like animals," she said. "Without consent, they just wanted to stop women from giving birth or having children. It was a very inhumane act."

A doctor, she added, later told her complications from the coil had left her unable to become pregnant. She went on to adopt two children from Colombia.

"We are very deferential to authority because we are colonial children," she said.

Reacting to the reports on Friday, Frederiksen said: "We will handle the political process together with the government of Greenland. The most important thing for me is that we find the right path together."

Greenland was a Danish colony until 1953 and did not gain home rule until 1979. Copenhagen continued to oversee its healthcare system until 1992.

The Inuit, or mixed Danish and Inuit, make up nearly 90% of the island's population of 56,000.

The birth-control campaign was designed to control the territory's population, which had ballooned since the 1950s, aided by modernisation and better healthcare. This growth, in addition to an increasing rate of teenage pregnancies, had alarmed the Danish authorities.

In 1970, the campaign was considered a "success" as fertility rates had fallen sharply, though the rate continued to fall for some time after that. In the eight years from the campaign's inception in 1966 until 1974 when it levelled off, Greenland's fertility rate plunged from seven children per woman to 2.3.

articles.title: Viral video of homeless encampment around city of Berkeley sparks safety concerns from parent
articles.summary: A viral video shows a homeless encampment near UC Berkeley student housing in Albany, California, sparking debate over campus safety and city responses.
articles.body: A homeless encampment located near University of California (UC), Berkeley student housing in Berkeley, California, went viral on X after a parent posted a video of what she witnessed while moving her child into an apartment. Lyanne Melendez, a longtime reporter for San Francisco's ABC7 News, shared the video after dropping off her son at University Village, a university-owned housing complex located in neighboring Albany. "I just dropped my son off at @UCBerkeley housing and as we were approaching we saw this behind his apartments," Melendez wrote on X, calling out the city of Berkeley, the city of Albany and Berkeley administration. UCLA SORORITIES HIRE PRIVATE SECURITY AMID TERRIFYING HARASSMENT BY HOMELESS MEN: REPORT While the housing complex sits within Albany city limits, the proximity to campus facilities has drawn reactions from students who navigate surrounding encampments daily. "The [encampment] is not on University property ... and we have no jurisdiction or ability to address this issue. Please contact the City of Berkeley," a UC Berkeley spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "Turns out it's not really right next to the main UC Berkeley campus, so that's an important thing to note, but there are still issues," John Paul Leon, a UC Berkeley student, told Fox News Digital. Leon, a senior double-majoring in economics and philosophy with a minor in public policy, told Fox News Digital seeing homeless individuals is a daily reality for students, even if it startles visiting families. "One of the normal things I go through every day is walking past three homeless people on my way to class," Leon said. "It's just a usual occurrence. It's something I've gotten used to, but I'm sure it's something that a lot of parents would not feel right about their children being subject to." FURIOUS RESIDENTS CONFRONT HOMELESS HOUSING LEADERS AS POPULAR BEACH COMMUNITY HITS BREAKING POINT Leon added that he believes university administrators are motivated to address the issue in ways that clear encampments from campus property and surrounding streets while directing individuals toward resources. Nearby business owners have also voiced frustration over conditions along the corridor. Emily Winston, founder and CEO of Berkeley-based Boichik Bagels, told Fox News Digital the conditions around the corner from her headquarters resemble a "slum out of a Third World country." "There's been feces found all over on various properties. It's been found on our property. I've had to clean it up personally before. Needles, very scary threats to staff that work in the different businesses here," Winston said. She added that the encampment sometimes takes up the "entirety of the sidewalk." Winston, who opened up the Sixth Street location in 2023, said she’s seen onsite sales drop as families avoid the area. "We have this awesome patio. We say, 'Come get a bagel and watch our robots make bagels.’ It's a fun family sort of event," Winston said. "And strangely enough, people don't want to bring their kids around the corner from this because it's pretty scary." SOCIALIST MAYORAL CANDIDATE IGNITES ONLINE MOCKERY FOR TOUTING BASIC CITY SERVICE She also said employees have been forced to navigate dangerous or unsettling encounters. "My staff had to beg someone to get out of our dumpster. They had actually gone in our dumpster and closed the lid on top of them," Winston recounted to Fox News Digital. "No one on my staff should be picking up human excrement from the sidewalk in front of our property or used needles. This is not what I built this business here to do." Winston called the corridor a "dystopian scene" and said she regretted choosing the location. "Had I known what was [going to] happen ... I probably would not have signed this lease, and I would have built this elsewhere," Winston said. She urged city leaders to clear the encampment permanently. "We're all paying rent. We're paying very significant fees and trying hard to make successful, thriving businesses here," she said. "And this is just, it’s rough, and it’s really exhausting. And it’s just gone on way too long." Winston and other local businesses joined a lawsuit against the city in 2024 over corridor conditions. She said city officials have told her "their hands are tied" because of lawsuits challenging encampment sweeps but compared the city's actions to housekeeping that only temporarily tidies up. "I know it's frustrating for them," she added. Barry Braden, co-founder and CEO of Fieldwork Brewing Co. on Sixth Street, told Fox News Digital the encampment has created ongoing challenges for businesses. "Fieldwork Brewing is deeply concerned about the ongoing conditions surrounding the encampment on Harrison Street and the impact they are having on our employees, our customers, neighboring businesses and the broader community," Braden said. "We recognize that homelessness is a complex issue requiring compassion and meaningful solutions, but the current situation has created persistent public safety, sanitation and access concerns that cannot be ignored." Braden said the brewery has been in contact with Berkeley officials and is asking city leaders to take action. "We have been in communication with the City of Berkeley and are asking City leaders to take prompt, effective action that both connects individuals in the encampment with appropriate services and restores a safe, clean and accessible environment for everyone who lives, works and visits the area," he told Fox News Digital. KAREN BASS GRILLED OVER BROKEN HOMELESSNESS PROMISE, BLAMES BUREAUCRACY FOR SLOWED PROGRESS In response to inquiries regarding local encampments, a spokesperson for the City of Berkeley highlighted ongoing municipal and legal efforts to address public health and safety concerns. "The city has methodically laid out its work in the area and our efforts to comply with court orders in numerous filings with the court," the spokesperson told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We were recently in front of the judge on August 13, and numerous declarations were filed in advance of that hearing. These declarations include extensive documentation of conditions on the street. If you review those records, you will gain insight into all that we are doing to address the encampments and address the public health and safety concerns," the spokesperson added. Melendez did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

articles.title: Who is Milo Yiannopoulos, far-right British commentator, detained by ICE? Former Trump supporter faces deportation
articles.summary: US News: British far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos who has been a vocal supporter of President Donald Trump has been detained by ICE in Louisiana. The De.
articles.body: British far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos who has been a vocal supporter of President Donald Trump has been detained by ICE in Louisiana. The Department of Homeland Security said Milo entered the country legally in 2019 but then overstayed, violating the laws.Who is Milo Yiannopoulos?41-year-old Milo calls himself the "most fabulous supervillain on the internet". He was an editor of US website Breitbart and also worked with rapper Kanye West. He was an early supporter of Trump during the 2016 election, headlining an event called Gays for Trump during the Republican National Convention that year, and has backed Trump's tighter immigration restrictions in the US.Yiannopoulos also worked with Nick Fuentes and former MAGA Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene. Yiannopoulos was credited with arranging West’s hugely controversial Mar-a-Lago dinner with Donald Trump and white nationalist Fuentes in 2022.Months earlier, in June 2025, he called for ICE to initiate on-the-spot deportations for anyone who could not prove their legal status during a stop by federal agents. He attached a photo to the post that read, “papers please.” “California needs ICE checkpoints at supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersections and government buildings, with on-the-spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally,” he wrote.Yiannopoulos was openly gay for years and married a man in Hawaii in 2017. However, he said in 2021 that he was attempting to “pray the gay away” or live as “ex-gay,” declaring that he was now straight.Yiannopoulos told the anti-LGBTQ outlet LIFE Site that year, “The guy I live with has been demoted to housemate, which hasn’t been easy for either of us. It helps that I can still just about afford to keep him in Givenchy and a new Porsche every year.”Laura Loomer celebrated Milo's detention and said he would be deported as he was living in the US illegally. “I was the first person to report on the fact that Milo was in the US illegally, where he incited violence against President Trump and worked for Marjorie Traitor Greene,” she wrote. “Recently, Candace Owens invited this illegal alien into her home. When Milo called for me to be assassinated, I reported him to ICE and the FBI. I told you all that Milo was an illegal alien.”She added, “Milo is going to be deported back to the UK, where he can live among the Muslims he has recently chosen to embrace. Today is a great day for America.”DHS statement on Milo Yiannopoulos' detention"On August 27, ICE arrested Milo Yiannopoulos, an illegal alien from the United Kingdom, at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport (MSY) in Kenner, Louisiana. Yiannopoulos legally entered the country on May 14, 2019, through New York City, New York. He chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws," the department said."Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an Immigration Judge on July 22, after failing to show up for his immigration hearing. He will remain in ICE custody pending removal.""Being in detention is a choice. We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App. The United States is offering illegal aliens $3,000 and a free flight to self-deport now. We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the US the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return," DHS said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
